issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, these two items directly contradict each other: being able to talk about the trauma very easily is inconsistent with losing the thread and being unable to finish when trying to explain it. Partial clarity could coexist with fragmented recall, but not with both easy verbal access and marked inability to narrate the event.

vignette:
# James

James was thirty-two years old when he came to the clinic, though the lines around his eyes and the careful way he held his shoulders made him seem older. He had worked as a park ranger for eight years, a job that had suited him—solitary, structured, outdoors—until the morning in late September when everything changed.

He had been conducting a routine patrol near the northern boundary of the state park, an area he knew intimately. The trail was empty, the forest quiet except for the sound of his boots on gravel. He remembered stopping to photograph a stand of birch trees for the park's newsletter. He remembered the light. He remembered, with excruciating clarity, the moment a van pulled up behind him and three men emerged. What came after existed in his mind as fragments: the sensation of being forced into the vehicle, the smell of diesel and sweat, the sound of a door sliding shut. There were hours—he could not say how many—of being restrained, questioned about park access routes and ranger schedules, struck repeatedly, threatened. He could not articulate the specifics of what they did to him, could not seem to hold the sequence of events in his mind long enough to explain it to anyone. Some moments burned with perfect, unbearable clarity: the face of one man, the texture of rope around his wrists, a particular phrase repeated in a voice he still heard in the dark. Other stretches of time were simply gone, erased, leaving only a sense of violation and terror that had no narrative shape.

He had been released near a highway. A trucker found him and called the police. The men were never caught.

In the months that followed, James had returned to work, but the park had become unrecognizable. Every delay in communication from headquarters sent his mind spiraling into catastrophe—if a supervisor didn't respond to a radio call within minutes, James was certain something had happened, that he was in danger, that the men had returned. He began checking the locks on his cabin obsessively, sometimes waking at three in the morning to verify that windows were secured, his hands moving through the ritual even as some part of him recognized its irrationality. His body had developed its own logic. Sounds that meant nothing—a vehicle backfiring, a knock on the door—would send his heart racing, his muscles tensed for violence, before his conscious mind had even registered what he had heard.

Driving became impossible. The vulnerability of being enclosed in a moving vehicle, unable to control his surroundings or escape, was intolerable. He had tried to ride as a passenger with colleagues, but the moment the door closed, panic would flood through him. He began making excuses, calling in sick when field assignments required transport, eventually requesting desk work that kept him in the station. His supervisor had noticed. There were conversations about his reliability, about whether he was still suited to the job.

James had come to believe that his body had been fundamentally broken by what happened to him. He felt weak in ways that had nothing to do with physical strength—his nervous system seemed to have turned against him, responding to phantom threats, unable to trust its own signals. More frightening than the hypervigilance itself was what it might mean. He lay awake at night convinced that his reactions—the checking, the avoidance, the way he rehearsed conversations with colleagues before they happened, as if he could script safety into existence—were signs that he was losing his mind. The thought that he might be going crazy terrified him more than the memory of the trauma itself.

He had stopped seeing friends. He numbed himself, moving through days in a kind of fog, unable to feel much of anything beyond the constant low hum of threat. When people tried to reach out, he pulled away. He had come to understand that other people could not be trusted, that relying on anyone was a vulnerability he could not afford. Even his therapist, he suspected, would not truly understand.

It was his sister who finally insisted he seek help. She had noticed him disappearing, had confronted him about the way he flinched at ordinary sounds, had refused to accept his insistence that he was fine. He had come to the clinic because she had given him an ultimatum, not because he believed anyone could help. What he wanted most was to feel safe again, to drive without terror, to sleep without checking locks. What he feared most was that the person he had become—fragmented, hypervigilant, isolated—was permanent, that the men who had tortured him had succeeded in breaking something in him that could never be repaired.
